questions.stem: Which ions do acids form when dissolved in water?

options.explanation: Acids in aqueous solution are a source of hydrogen ions, and these make the solution acidic.
Hydroxide ions come from alkalis, not acids.
Oxide ions appear in molten electrolysis chemistry, not in aqueous acids.

options.text: No ions form until the water is heated
options.explanation: Dissolving releases the ions at room temperature; heating is not required.

questions.stem: What do alkalis release when added to water?

options.explanation: Alkalis in aqueous solution are a source of hydroxide ions, which make the solution alkaline.
Hydrogen ions belong to acids; releasing them would make the water acidic.
Water is the solvent; the alkali adds hydroxide ions to it.
Free electrons belong to metal lattices; solutions carry ions instead.

questions.stem: What does the pH scale actually measure?

options.text: The amount of hydrogen ions present in the solution
options.explanation: The note defines pH as a measure of the hydrogen ion amount, which is why acids read low.

options.text: How dangerous the solution is to touch
options.explanation: Hazard is not what pH reports; the ion concentration is.
Temperature is unrelated to the pH reading described here.

options.text: The total volume of liquid present
options.explanation: Volume has no part in the pH definition.

questions.stem: Why does hydrochloric acid solution turn litmus red?

options.text: Because the dissolved acid releases hydrogen ions into the water
options.explanation: The released H+ ions make the solution acidic, and litmus signals acidity with red.

options.text: Because hydrochloric acid contains chloride ions
options.explanation: Chloride ions are spectators here; it is the hydrogen ions that set the acidity.

options.text: Because litmus reacts to the green colour of the solution
options.explanation: The solution is colourless; litmus responds to acidity, not to colour.
Pure water is neutral; the acid added to it supplies the hydrogen ions.

questions.stem: A solution reads pH 13 on the scale. What does it contain plenty of?

options.text: Hydroxide ions, OH-, making it strongly alkaline
options.explanation: A high pH means plentiful hydroxide ions, and 11 to 14 is the strong alkali band.

options.text: Hydrogen ions, H+, making it strongly acidic
options.explanation: Plentiful hydrogen ions would push the reading towards 0, not 13.

options.text: Neither ion type, since 13 is neutral
options.explanation: Neutral is 7; 13 sits deep in the alkaline band.
Pure water reads pH 7; a reading of 13 requires dissolved alkali.

questions.stem: What is produced when H+ ions meet OH- ions?

options.explanation: The hydrogen ion and hydroxide ion combine to give a water molecule, which is the heart of neutralisation.
Hydrogen gas forms with metals, not when the two ions combine.
Carbon dioxide belongs to carbonate reactions; no carbon is involved here.
A salt forms alongside the water in a full equation, but the ions themselves make water.
options.misconception: salt mistaken for the ionic product

questions.stem: Which is the net ionic equation for every acid-base neutralisation?

options.explanation: This single line covers all such neutralisations and explains why the result can be neutral.
That re-forms an acid; neutralisation removes the ions into water.
That dissolves an alkali; it is not the neutralisation step.

questions.stem: Why is magnesium reacting with hydrochloric acid not a neutralisation?

options.text: A salt forms but no water is made
options.explanation: The definition of neutralisation needs the water-forming ion pairing, which the metal reaction lacks.

options.text: Because magnesium is too unreactive to count
options.explanation: Magnesium reacts readily; the classification fails on the missing water, not on vigour.

options.text: Because no salt forms in the reaction
options.explanation: A salt does form; it is the absence of water that excludes the reaction.

options.text: Because the acid is not concentrated enough
options.explanation: Concentration plays no part in whether the reaction is called a neutralisation.

questions.stem: What are the products when hydrochloric acid neutralises sodium hydroxide?

options.explanation: The ions swap to give the salt sodium chloride plus the water made from H+ and OH-.
Hydrogen gas belongs to metal-plus-acid reactions; neutralisation makes water.
Neither product appears in this reaction; the pair is salt and water.
Those are the reactants, not the products.

questions.stem: Why do farmers add limestone or quicklime to fields?

options.text: The bases neutralise acidic soil, raising the pH for crops that dislike low values
options.explanation: Neutralisation in the field lifts the soil pH, since some crops cannot tolerate values below 7.

options.text: To make the soil more acidic for special plants
options.explanation: The additions are bases, so they raise pH rather than lower it.

options.text: To add metal salts as fertiliser
options.explanation: The purpose named is pH adjustment, not fertilising.

options.text: To kill all the organisms in the soil
options.explanation: Nothing in the treatment targets soil life; it corrects acidity.
